title: Easily Confused
blurb: Understand speech with omitted consonant sounds

steps.html:
A lamp post you have walked past a thousand times is suddenly covered in knitted wool. Nobody saw it happen, because it was done at two in the morning. Plus the words English speakers confuse — and the ones you will mishear if you are not expecting them.

  • Work out what was said when consonants disappear
  • Follow a feature on a street-art movement
  • Tell loose from lose, and specially from especially
  • Write about a form of street art

A fault is the thing that is wrong. To fix is to repair it.

The act of learning something so that you can repeat it exactly.

To watch or check something over a period of time.

Something done wrongly. You make a mistake — never do one.

steps.title: Before you listen: why do consonants disappear in fast speech?
options: Because a /t/ or /d/ between two other consonants is hard to say quickly, so it drops.
Because the words are being shortened deliberately.
steps.answer: Because a /t/ or /d/ between two other consonants is hard to say quickly, so it drops.
steps.why: I'm not going comes out as something closer to I'm noh going. Nothing is wrong; it is simply what fluent speech does.

steps.title: Language noticing.
steps.sub: 'It is believed to have started in the United States.'
steps.prompt: Why does the writer use this form rather than 'People believe it started…'?
options: It reports a widely held view without claiming who holds it or that it is certain.
It is the only correct form after believe.
steps.answer: It reports a widely held view without claiming who holds it or that it is certain.
steps.why: It is believed / said / thought that… is the standard passive for reporting something without taking responsibility for it.

steps.title: Read between the lines.
steps.sub: The feature says the point is to put something handmade into an industrial environment.
steps.prompt: What does that phrasing imply about where the practice is done?
options: That it works anywhere, indoors or out.
That the setting is part of the meaning: the same object in a craft fair would say nothing.
That the makers dislike industrial materials.
steps.answer: That the setting is part of the meaning: the same object in a craft fair would say nothing.
steps.why: If the contrast carries the meaning, the location is not decoration. That is why it appears on lamp posts and not in galleries.

steps.title: Three structures that look alike
steps.html:
Nothing new. This is Lessons 25 and 26 put side by side, because learners mix them.

Passive: the subject receives the action, and it is not clear or not important who did it. The cover was removed overnight.

Causative: you arranged for somebody to do it. The council had the cover removed. Notice that the object comes between had and the participle.

Reporting passive: It is believed / said / thought / reported that…, or It is believed to have started in the United States. Use it when you are passing on a view that is widely held but not attributable.

The test that separates the first two: does the sentence say who arranged it? The walls were taken down — no. The company had its walls taken down — yes, the company arranged it.

And the word order test for the causative: the thing always comes before the participle. had its walls taken down, never had taken down its walls, which would mean the company did the work itself.

steps.title: Example bank.
steps.html:
Ten sentences from the feature.

Trees and statues are finding themselves decorated.
An unusual reflexive, and a deliberate joke.

It is believed to have started in the United States.
Reporting passive, compact form.

It is often done secretly at night.
Passive; the doer is deliberately not named.

It can be easily removed.
Modal passive.

The cracks have been filled with knitted wool.
Present perfect passive.

The council had the covers removed.
Causative: the council arranged it.

They got them removed within a week.
Get, informal, same meaning.

Artists have teams of people assist them.
Causative with a person and a bare infinitive.

It is said that local governments dislike it.
The that version.

The council had removed the covers
Past perfect: the council did the work itself.

steps.title: Same event, three structures
steps.html:
1. The event: overnight, somebody took the knitted cover off a lamp post. The council paid for it.
  2. If you do not know or care who physically did it: The cover was removed overnight. Passive.
  3. If the point is that the council arranged it: The council had the cover removed. Causative — object before participle.
  4. If you are passing on a rumour: It is believed that the council had it removed. Reporting passive wrapped around the causative.
  5. And the trap: The council had removed the cover is a past perfect and means the councillors did it with their own hands, which is a different story.

steps.title: You are going to write about street art.

options.label: A piece of street art near you
Why cities remove some street art and keep other pieces
Something you would put in a public space

steps.title: Write your piece.
steps.sub: 140–170 words. Use at least four passive forms and at least one causative.
steps.html:
• Say what was done, and when, in the passive.
  • Use <i>it is believed</i> for anything you cannot attribute.
  • Say what the authorities did about it, using the causative.
  • Close with what happened next.

Useful language

  • It is believed to have started in …
  • It is often done at night, because …
  • The work was removed within … , and nobody knows who …
  • The council had it taken down.
  • Unlike graffiti, it can be easily removed.
  • It is very much about making … more beautiful.
steps.modelHtml:
The bridge on Erzhanov Street

The railings on the footbridge were covered in knitted wool one night last April. Nobody has ever admitted to doing it, and it is believed to have been the work of a group rather than one person, because the whole bridge was finished before six in the morning.

It stayed for eleven days. Then the council had it removed, on the grounds that wet wool holds water against metal and the railings would rust.

That was probably true, and it was also beside the point. Nothing else on that bridge had been repainted in fifteen years. Unlike graffiti, the covers could be taken off in an afternoon and left nothing behind.

Two weeks later somebody knitted a single small square and attached it to the same railing. It has not been removed.
